checkpoint_mismatch.checkpoint: checkpoints.2: "A hairdryer has a power of 2000 W. A kettle has a power of 2500 W. Which transfers more energy each second?"
checkpoint_mismatch.key_point: keyPoints[2] "Power in everyday contexts": "Hairdryer: ~2000 W (2 kW). Electric kettle: ~2000–3000 W."
checkpoint_mismatch.why: The checkpoint tests the definition of power as energy transferred per second. That definition is taught in keyPoints[0] ("It is how much energy transfer happens per second"), not in keyPoints[2]. keyPoints[2] only lists typical values and never states that a higher wattage means more joules per second. So the answer is supported by a different key point from the one the checkpoint sits with.

not_checked: The typical power values in keyPoints[2].content, keyPoints[2].writeBullets, tables[0] and revisionCardBullets (for example "Human body at rest: ~80 W", "Walking: ~300 W", "Large power station: ~1–2 GW", "Small power station ~500 MW ... hundreds of thousands of homes") are not in the specification sections. I could only check them as broadly plausible orders of magnitude from own knowledge. The cycling figures are also given inconsistently: "~100–400 W" in keyPoints[2].content, "~150 W" for recreational cycling in tables[0], and "~150–400 W" in revisionCardBullets.

examTips[2] ("If a question gives you efficiency and power together, find the useful output power. It equals efficiency × input power.") relates to efficiency, which is not in the specification sections provided. It could not be checked against the given spec text, although it is correct physics.

The specification's 'Key opportunities for skills development' references (MS 3b, c; MS 1c; WS 4.5) are not defined in the text provided, so I could not check whether the lesson covers the skills they refer to.

The historical claim in keyPoints[2].content about steam engines in the Industrial Revolution ("giving out many kilowatts non-stop") is outside the specification and was checked only loosely against own knowledge.
